newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU stepping up pressure on telecoms liberalisation.
newsitem.headline: EU stepping up pressure on telecoms liberalisation.

text.p: The European Commission plans to announce on Thursday that it will step up pressure on national governments to open their telecommunications markets on schedule.
With the European Union's January 1, 1998 deadline for full liberalisation approaching, the Commission will publish a "report card" outlining how well each country has implemented EU rules.
The report gives the lowest marks to Belgium, Greece, Portugal and Spain, while highlighting problems in Austria, Ireland, Italy and Luxembourg.

A draft obtained by Reuters warns that the Commission will use "expedited" procedures for bringing cases to the European Court of Justice when liberalisation measures are implemented late or improperly.
The report covers a package of EU directives requiring governments to open their markets in areas ranging from satellite and mobile communications to leased lines and basic voice phone service.
Britain, Denmark, Finland and Sweden got top scores, having implemented "virtually the entire package", it says.
Belgium is at the other end of the scale, with only three of 39 envisaged liberalisation measures actually adopted.

Greece also makes a poor showing, having failed to enact EU rules on sectors including satellite communications, mobile phones and cable TV. It agreed a timetable for implementing those measures with the Commission in April.
The Commission is expected to rule later this month on a request by Athens to wait until 2003 to fully liberalise its market.

The Commission has already officially agreed that Luxembourg can wait until July 1998, and Ireland and Portugal until 2000 to introduce full competition. Spain promised open markets by end-November 1998 in a deal that won Commission approval of Telefonica de Espana's participation in the Unisource telecoms alliance.
EU states agreed those countries could take more time because they had small or less developed networks. However, they have lagged even in areas where delays have not been approved.

The report says a "considerable quantity" of legislation needs to be adopted in Spain, while Portugal has failed to implement properly rules on leased lines and imposes improper licensing requirements on corporate phone networks.

EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert was hard on Italy during a visit to Rome on Tuesday, saying it had missed deadlines for liberalising telecoms infrastructure and notifying the Commission of legislation on voice telephone.
In addition to taking legal action when EU rules are not turned into national law, the Commission said it planned to monitor the way the measures are actually applied in the market.
It said it had taken a number of internal measures, including setting up a team to monitor the situation.
